summary:
Khabarovsk Krai stands under the national framework of Russia, which since 2023 has prohibited legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care outright. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the Supreme Court's November 2023 designation of the "international LGBT movement" as extremist supplies the charge on which courts now convict. The "gay propaganda" statute carries fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution.

The US State Department travel advisory for Russia advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics. It states that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported, and that displaying certain symbols, including the rainbow flag, is a crime. A trans visitor therefore faces administrative detention and removal on top of the underlying penalties that apply to residents.

Human Rights Watch recorded, as of 30 June 2025, 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in the designated "International LGBT Movement" or displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with sentences reaching 12 years in prison. The same report documents 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024 for displaying banned symbols, mostly on social media, which places online posting and shared images within the enforcement surface rather than outside it.

No Khabarovsk Krai-specific trans detention, prosecution or violence figures appear in the inventory. The one local incident it carries is a measure of how gender nonconformity is treated in the territory: a biology and chemistry teacher in Khabarovsk was forced to resign in September after video of him dancing in high heels surfaced amid public controversy, and in October he filed a lawsuit against the Khabarovsk education department seeking reinstatement, a case still ongoing when the UK Home Office documented it.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch reports 257 "gay propaganda" penalties imposed across Russia in 2023-24 against 22 in 2021-22, and article 20.3 symbol cases overwhelmingly arising from social media posts. The escalation is in volume as well as severity, and the two-year comparison sets the direction a visitor entering Khabarovsk Krai should expect enforcement to run.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression for Russia (June 2025) is the framework this territory is assessed under. Its national figures record at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024, and it affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.

The absence of criminal liability for consensual same-sex activity distinguishes Russia's position from jurisdictions that punish intimacy directly, but the extremism designation and the propaganda statute reach public expression, symbols and online content instead, so the practical exposure for a visitor is administrative detention, deportation and confiscation-level scrutiny of devices and displayed items.
localsOnly:
Residents of Khabarovsk Krai are subject to the same 2023 prohibitions on legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care as visitors, with no territorial exemption in the sources: there is no legal route to amend sex markers on Russian documents and no lawful provision of trans-specific medical care.

The Khabarovsk education department became a defendant in October when the resigning teacher sued for reinstatement, following the September forced resignation prompted by the high-heels video. Employment consequences for perceived gender nonconformity are therefore documented locally, not only in the national press.

Residents face both administrative liability under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, most often on social media, and criminal extremism charges carrying sentences of up to 12 years. Community members who document or share rainbow imagery, pride symbols or content construed as endorsing gender transition carry exposure in both channels.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Khabarovsk Krai-specific data on trans homicides, police violence, detention conditions, access to hormones or passport-amendment refusals is present in the inventory; the territory's profile rests on the national framework plus a single local employment incident. Whether local enforcement deviates from the national pattern in either direction is unresolved on these sources.

The outcome of the Khabarovsk teacher's reinstatement lawsuit is unresolved: the UK Home Office note records it as ongoing as of June 2025, and no later ruling is sourced here. The inventory gives the months of the resignation and filing as September and October without stating the year in the claim text, so the year of those events is not sourced.

Whether a visitor's personal belongings, device images or private messages would be treated as "display" under article 20.3 is not addressed by the sources; the advisory's symbol language is stated for display generally, and the article 20.3 cases cited concern social media posting. This distinction is unresolved rather than settled in either direction.
